# Data visualization {#sec-visualization}

Julia has three reasonable routes to graphics, all resting on
[**Makie.jl**](https://docs.makie.org) [@danisch2021makie]:

| Route | For whom |
|---|---|
| `TidierPlots.jl` | people coming from `ggplot2` who want the same grammar |
| `AlgebraOfGraphics.jl` | people who want an idiomatically Julian grammar of graphics |
| Plain `Makie.jl` | full control over the figure |

This chapter shows all three on the same data, because the right choice depends on the
task — and because knowing how to translate between them keeps you from getting stuck.

```{julia}
#| label: setup-06
using TidierData
using CairoMakie
using AlgebraOfGraphics
using CSV, DataFrames

CairoMakie.activate!(type = "png")

ponds = CSV.read(joinpath("..", "data", "ponds.csv"), DataFrame)
ponds_c = @chain ponds begin
    @drop_missing(canopy)
    @mutate(log_area = log(area_m2))
end

nrow(ponds_c)
```

::: {.callout-note .exercise}
## Exercises in this chapter

A figure cannot be checked automatically, so in most *Your turn* boxes you compare
your plot with the one in the solution. Start each session by loading the packages and
the data, with the book folder open in VS Code:

```julia
include("exercises/check.jl")
using TidierData, TidierPlots, CairoMakie, AlgebraOfGraphics, CSV, DataFrames, Statistics
ponds = CSV.read(joinpath("data", "ponds.csv"), DataFrame)
ponds_c = @chain ponds begin
    @drop_missing(canopy)
    @mutate(log_area = log(area_m2))
end
```
:::

## `TidierPlots.jl`: the ggplot grammar {#sec-tidierplots}

```{julia}
#| label: fig-tidierplots-scatter
#| fig-cap: "Richness against canopy cover, by region."
using TidierPlots

ggplot(ponds_c, @aes(x = canopy, y = richness, color = region)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
    labs(x = "Canopy cover (%)", y = "Species richness",
         title = "Richness declines with shading")
```

::: {.r-equivalent}
**In R**

```r
ggplot(ponds_c, aes(x = canopy, y = richness, colour = region)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(x = "Canopy cover (%)", y = "Species richness")
```

The translation is nearly character for character; the difference is the `@` in
`@aes`.
:::

::: {.callout-note .exercise}
## Your turn 6.1 — Richness and temperature

Redo @fig-tidierplots-scatter with water temperature (`temp_c`) on the x axis and the
points coloured by hydroperiod (`hydro`). Label both axes. Does richness change with
temperature as clearly as with canopy?

There is no checker for this one: compare your figure with the one in the solution.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint

Only the `@aes` mapping and the labels change.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{julia}
#| label: answer-6-1
ggplot(ponds_c, @aes(x = temp_c, y = richness, color = hydro)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
    labs(x = "Water temperature (°C)", y = "Species richness")
```

The cloud is much flatter than for canopy. The simulation does include a temperature
effect (`scripts/make_data.jl`), but a small one: about 3% more species per degree,
invisible next to the scatter between ponds.
:::
:::

## `AlgebraOfGraphics.jl`: an algebraic grammar {#sec-aog}

AoG treats plots as an algebra: `*` combines layers, `+` superimposes them.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-aog-scatter
#| fig-cap: "The same plot in AlgebraOfGraphics, with a linear fit per region."
plt = AlgebraOfGraphics.data(ponds_c) *
      mapping(:canopy => "Canopy cover (%)",
              :richness => "Species richness",
              color = :region => "Region") *
      (visual(Scatter, alpha = 0.6) + AlgebraOfGraphics.linear())

draw(plt; figure = (size = (700, 450),))
```

::: {.callout-note}
`AlgebraOfGraphics.data` and `AlgebraOfGraphics.linear` are qualified because the
names `data` and `linear` collide with other loaded packages. In a script using only
AoG, `data(...)` and `linear()` suffice.
:::

::: {.callout-note .exercise}
## Your turn 6.2 — Body size, with fitted lines

With AlgebraOfGraphics, plot `body_size` against `temp_c`, coloured by `hydro`, with a
linear fit for each hydroperiod. Do permanent and temporary ponds differ?

There is no checker for this one: compare your figure with the one in the solution.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint

Start from the block above and change the `mapping`. The fitted lines follow the
colour grouping automatically.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{julia}
#| label: answer-6-2
plt = AlgebraOfGraphics.data(ponds_c) *
      mapping(:temp_c => "Water temperature (°C)",
              :body_size => "Body size (mm)",
              color = :hydro => "Hydroperiod") *
      (visual(Scatter, alpha = 0.6) + AlgebraOfGraphics.linear())

draw(plt; figure = (size = (700, 450),))
```

The two lines almost coincide: in the simulation, body size depends on temperature and
canopy but not on hydroperiod. We test this formally in @sec-linear-models.
:::
:::

## Facets {#sec-facets}

```{julia}
#| label: fig-facets
#| fig-cap: "Richness–area relationship faceted by hydroperiod."
plt = AlgebraOfGraphics.data(ponds_c) *
      mapping(:log_area => "log(area)",
              :richness => "Richness",
              color = :region,
              layout = :hydro) *
      (visual(Scatter, alpha = 0.6) + AlgebraOfGraphics.linear())

draw(plt; figure = (size = (800, 400),))
```

::: {.callout-note .exercise}
## Your turn 6.3 — Facets in the ggplot grammar

Translate @fig-facets to `TidierPlots.jl`, using `facet_wrap` to split the panels by
hydroperiod. Leave out the fitted lines (see the warning in the solution).

There is no checker for this one: compare your figure with the one in the solution.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint

`facet_wrap(facets = :hydro)` is added with `+`, like any other layer.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{julia}
#| label: answer-6-3
ggplot(ponds_c, @aes(x = log_area, y = richness, color = region)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
    facet_wrap(facets = :hydro) +
    labs(x = "log(area)", y = "Richness")
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## A limit of TidierPlots

In `TidierPlots.jl` 1.0.0 (checked in September 2026), adding
`geom_smooth(method = "lm")` to a faceted plot fails with
`column name :facet not found`. `geom_smooth` works without facets, and facets work
without `geom_smooth`, but not together. When the ggplot grammar reaches a limit like
this, AlgebraOfGraphics (@fig-facets) is the way out.
:::
:::
:::

## Distributions {#sec-distributions}

```{julia}
#| label: fig-boxplot
#| fig-cap: "Richness distribution by region and hydroperiod."
plt = AlgebraOfGraphics.data(ponds_c) *
      mapping(:region => "Region",
              :richness => "Richness",
              color = :hydro => "Hydroperiod",
              dodge = :hydro) *
      visual(BoxPlot)

draw(plt; figure = (size = (700, 420),))
```

::: {.callout-note .exercise}
## Your turn 6.4 — The shape of a distribution

Boxplots hide the shape of a distribution. Show the distribution of `body_size` in each
region as violins (`Violin`), with one colour per region.

There is no checker for this one: compare your figure with the one in the solution.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint

Replace `BoxPlot` with `Violin` and map `region` to both the x axis and `color`.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{julia}
#| label: answer-6-4
plt = AlgebraOfGraphics.data(ponds_c) *
      mapping(:region => "Region",
              :body_size => "Body size (mm)",
              color = :region) *
      visual(Violin)

draw(plt; figure = (size = (700, 420),))
```
:::
:::

## Plain `Makie.jl`: full control {#sec-makie}

When a figure needs a layout the grammar cannot express, drop down to Makie.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-makie-composite
#| fig-cap: "A composite figure assembled by hand with Makie."
fig = Figure(size = (860, 380))

ax1 = Axis(fig[1, 1], xlabel = "Canopy cover (%)", ylabel = "Richness",
           title = "(a) Canopy")
scatter!(ax1, ponds_c.canopy, ponds_c.richness, color = (:steelblue, 0.6))

ax2 = Axis(fig[1, 2], xlabel = "log(area)", ylabel = "Richness",
           title = "(b) Area")
scatter!(ax2, ponds_c.log_area, ponds_c.richness, color = (:darkorange, 0.6))

ax3 = Axis(fig[1, 3], xlabel = "Richness", ylabel = "Frequency",
           title = "(c) Distribution")
hist!(ax3, ponds_c.richness, bins = 12, color = (:seagreen, 0.7))

fig
```

Makie's layout system is grid-based (`fig[row, col]`), covering the role of
`patchwork` and `cowplot` in R without an extra package.

::: {.callout-note .exercise}
## Your turn 6.5 — Two panels by hand

Build a figure with `size = (800, 350)` and two panels: on the left, a boxplot of
richness by region; on the right, a bar chart of the proportion of ponds with the focal
species in each region (the numbers from 5.4). Store it in `fig_regions`.

There is no checker for this one: compare your figure with the one in the solution.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint

Makie's `boxplot!` and `barplot!` want numbers on the x axis. Give each region a
number with `[findfirst(==(r), regs) for r in ponds.region]`, where
`regs = ["Amazon", "Atlantic", "Cerrado"]`, and put the names back with
`xticks = (1:3, regs)` in each `Axis`.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{julia}
#| label: answer-6-5
regs = ["Amazon", "Atlantic", "Cerrado"]
idx = [findfirst(==(r), regs) for r in ponds.region]
props = [mean(ponds.focal[ponds.region .== r]) for r in regs]

fig_regions = Figure(size = (800, 350))

ax1 = Axis(fig_regions[1, 1], xticks = (1:3, regs),
           xlabel = "Region", ylabel = "Richness", title = "(a) Richness")
boxplot!(ax1, idx, ponds.richness, color = (:steelblue, 0.6))

ax2 = Axis(fig_regions[1, 2], xticks = (1:3, regs),
           xlabel = "Region", ylabel = "Proportion of ponds", title = "(b) Focal species")
barplot!(ax2, 1:3, props, color = (:darkorange, 0.8))

fig_regions
```

The two panels tell different stories: richness differs sharply between regions,
focal-species occurrence hardly at all.
:::
:::

## Saving figures {#sec-saving}

```{julia}
#| label: saving
#| eval: false
save("figure.png", fig; px_per_unit = 3)   # high-resolution raster
save("figure.pdf", fig)                    # vector, for publication
save("figure.svg", fig)
```

::: {.callout-note .exercise}
## Your turn 6.6 — A figure for publication

Save `fig_regions` from 6.5 as `focal-by-region.png`, at three pixels per unit, in the
book folder. Then check the file: `check("6.6", "focal-by-region.png")`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint

The block above shows the keyword that sets the resolution.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{julia}
#| label: answer-6-6
#| eval: false
save("focal-by-region.png", fig_regions; px_per_unit = 3)
check("6.6", "focal-by-region.png")
```

An 800 × 350 figure at three pixels per unit gives a 2400 × 1050 px image — enough
for a two-column journal figure. For vector output, save as `.pdf` instead.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Choosing a backend

`CairoMakie` produces publication-quality static output (PNG, PDF, SVG) and is what
this book uses. `GLMakie` opens GPU-accelerated interactive windows — useful for
exploring data, unsuitable for rendering a book.
:::

## Challenges {.unnumbered}

1. In 6.1 you judged the temperature effect by eye. Add a linear fit per hydroperiod
   with `geom_smooth(method = "lm")`. Does the line change your reading of the plot?
   What would you need to know before trusting it?
2. Panel (b) of 6.5 shows proportions without uncertainty. Add an error bar of
   $\pm 2$ standard errors to each bar, with $\text{SE} = \sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$ and
   `errorbars!`. Do the regions still look different?
3. Redo @fig-makie-composite with one colour per region in every panel and a single
   shared legend on the right (`Legend(fig[1, 4], ...)`).
